people.name: Naw Louisa Benson Craig
body: In the 1950s, a young woman from Rangoon won the Miss Burma pageant twice. A few years later she was in command of Karen resistance troops. Her life runs through much of what happened to Karen people in the twentieth century.

Some background helps. The Karen are an ethnic people native to Burma, also known as Myanmar, and Thailand. The Minnesota Department of Health describes a civil war in Burma lasting more than 70 years, with Karen resistance groups fighting the Burmese military for autonomy. It drove many people into refugee camps on the Thai border, and in 2010 MPR News reported that more than 100,000 were still in those camps.

Louisa Benson was born in Rangoon in 1941 to a Jewish father and a Karen mother. After her pageant years she became a movie star. In 1964 she married Lin Htin, a Karen resistance leader. MPR News reports that he was assassinated during peace talks with the military government, and that she then took command of his troops. In 1967 she left Burma, married an American and settled in California. Her daughter has written that her reasons for leaving remain unclear.

In the United States she kept working for her people. MPR News reports that she promoted the resettlement program that brought many Karen families to the Twin Cities. The Karen American Communities Foundation, established in December 2007, names her as a founder and director. She died in February 2010, and her memorial was held in the Los Angeles area. Her daughter, the novelist Charmaine Craig, drew on two years of interviews with her for the novel Miss Burma.
keyFacts: 1941: Born in Rangoon, Burma, to a Jewish father and a Karen mother.
1950s: Twice won the Miss Burma pageant; later a film actress.
1964: Married Lin Htin, a Karen resistance leader; took command of his troops after his death.
1967: Left Burma and settled in California.
2007: A founder of the Karen American Communities Foundation.
February 2010: Died.
people.connectToWork: When a form or a conversation starts from the word "refugee", what might you miss about the rest of a person's life and work, and how would you ask?

people.name: Charmaine Craig
body: In 2017 a novel about a Karen family appeared on the longlist for the National Book Award for Fiction, one of the top literary prizes in the United States. Miss Burma follows a family through war, independence and exile, and it draws on the life of the author's mother, Louisa Benson Craig, who is also on this page.

Craig was born in the United States and grew up in Santa Monica. She has described her heritage as Karen, Jewish and white, and has said classmates often asked what she was and mistook "Karen" for "Korean". She worked as an actor before turning to fiction. Her novels are The Good Men (2002), Miss Burma (2017) and My Nemesis (2023). In 2018 Miss Burma was also longlisted for the Women's Prize for Fiction in the United Kingdom.

In 2017 she visited the Karen Organization of Minnesota, where staff recommended the book to the people they serve. As of October 2026, her publisher says she teaches in the fiction program at the University of California, Riverside, and lives in Los Angeles.
Her work shows one of the ways a family history can be carried: not through where someone lives, but through memory, interviews and a book.
keyFacts: Former actor; later a novelist.
2002: Debut novel, The Good Men.
2017: Miss Burma longlisted for the National Book Award for Fiction.
2018: Miss Burma longlisted for the Women's Prize for Fiction.
2023: Published My Nemesis.
Teaches fiction at UC Riverside.

people.name: Wilfred Tun Baw
body: Around 2000, Wilfred Tun Baw arrived in Minnesota with a small group of Karen refugees. MPR News described him as among the first Karen to reach the Twin Cities. He later told MPR that they lived in a church basement for nearly two months, and that only 12 to 15 Karen families lived in the state then. "It was very, very tough for us," he said. The pastor of First Baptist Church in downtown St. Paul told MPR that his church was where the Karen first took shelter.

It helps to know why a church basement was the starting point. MPR reported in 2010 that about half of the Karen who fled Myanmar were Baptists, a tie that went back to American Baptist missionaries, and that about half of First Baptist's congregation had become Karen by then.

As more families arrived, community leaders built a formal organization. With help from Vietnamese Social Services and members of the volunteer Karen Community of Minnesota, they created the Karen Organization of Minnesota, which received nonprofit status at the end of 2008. In 2009 it received its first grant money and hired Tun Baw as its first executive director. By KOM's account, about 3,000 Karen people lived in Minnesota that year, and KOM had four staff seeing 50 to 60 visitors a day.

In January 2010, Karen refugees filled Roseville Lutheran Church to celebrate Karen New Year, year 2749 on the Karen calendar, and Tun Baw spoke to reporters as KOM's leader. Later in 2010 he moved into a social service position at KOM, and Chong Bee Vang became executive director.
keyFacts: About 2000: Arrived in Minnesota and lived nearly two months in a church basement.
December 30, 2008: KOM received nonprofit status.
2009: Hired as KOM's first executive director.
January 2010: Spoke for KOM at Karen New Year, Roseville.
2010: Moved to a social service position at KOM.
people.connectToWork: Before you start outreach, what do you know about what people have already built for themselves, and how would you work alongside it rather than around it?

people.name: Marner Saw
people.field: Immigration services, elder programs, peace advocacy
body: When Eh Tah Khu arrived in Minnesota in 2010, one of the people who helped him was Marner Saw, who helped him enroll in English classes and county benefits. Eh Tah Khu would go on to co-lead the Karen Organization of Minnesota. According to KOM, Saw helped hundreds of refugee families start new lives in Minnesota and become citizens.

Saw was born in Burma in 1970 and spent time in a refugee camp in Thailand. He and his family lived in Minnesota from 2005. KOM describes him as one of its founders, and KSTP reported that he was among its first staff when it opened in 2009. He worked in immigration services and coordinated a program for elders. He was also a leader at Trinity Karen Baptist Church and with the Karen Community of Minnesota.
His commitment reached past Minnesota. He returned to Thailand several times to work with Karen leaders toward a ceasefire in Burma.

Marner Saw died on October 2, 2020, at age 50, from complications of COVID-19 after several weeks in the hospital. He was survived by his wife and four children. KOM remembered him as "a loving husband, brother, father, grandfather, and friend to many of us." Eh Tah Khu called his death "a big loss for the family and for the community."
keyFacts: 1970: Born in Burma; later lived in a Thai refugee camp.
2005: Settled in Minnesota with his family.
A founder of KOM; worked in immigration services and coordinated its elders' program.
Traveled to Thailand several times to support ceasefire efforts.
October 2, 2020: Died at age 50 of COVID-19 complications.
people.connectToWork: Who in your area already walks people through your system without being paid or named for it? What would it take to recognize that work and not lean on it?

people.name: Eh Tah Khu
body: In 2011, a year after arriving in Minnesota, Eh Tah Khu took a job as a youth development coordinator at the Karen Organization of Minnesota, as it was starting its first youth program. Five years later he was its co-executive director.

Khu was born in Burma and moved to Thailand as a refugee because of political conflict. He earned a four-year degree from Kawthoolei Karen Baptist Bible School and College, then spent two years teaching and helping manage schools under the Burmese Migrant Workers Education Committee. He came to Minnesota in 2010 with his wife and son, and in his first months he got help from Marner Saw, who is also on this page.

He became Youth and Social Services program manager in 2013, became a U.S. citizen in 2015, and was named co-executive director in February 2016. In 2023 Twin Cities Business described him as one of the first nonprofit executives of Karen descent in the country. It reported that KOM grew from 18 to 35 employees under him and that he led its team serving newly arrived Afghan and Ukrainian refugees.

When Ler Htoo was promoted to sergeant in 2024, Khu told MPR News, "With law enforcement action taken against minority ethnic groups [in Myanmar], there's a lot of mistrust." He said that knowing community members who work in law enforcement helps build trust. That is one person's account, from his own work.

In June 2025, KOM announced that he would step down as co-executive director as he neared 15 years there, to pursue new opportunities, and that he would stay through December 31, 2025. In November 2025 its board named Alice Buckner executive director, and as of October 2026 KOM's staff page does not list him. His term on the board of the Council on Asian Pacific Minnesotans runs from June 2025 to January 2028. The council's page, as saved in May 2026, still used his old KOM title.
keyFacts: 2010: Resettled in Minnesota with his wife and son.
2011: Joined KOM as a youth development coordinator; 2013: program manager.
2015: Became a U.S. citizen.
February 2016: Named KOM co-executive director.
June 2025: KOM announced he would step down, staying through December 31, 2025.
June 2025 to January 2028: Term on the Council on Asian Pacific Minnesotans board.
people.connectToWork: If someone seems cautious around your office or uniform, how would you find out what they have experienced with officials, without assuming either way?

people.name: Ler Htoo
body: In February 2024 the St. Paul Police Department promoted Ler Htoo to sergeant. He was the department's first sergeant of Karen descent, and the Pioneer Press described him as likely the highest-ranking Karen officer in Minnesota and the country. He told MPR News he hoped younger people could see him as a role model and come to him for help.
He spent his first three years in Myanmar and about the next fifteen in refugee camps in Thailand. At 18 he moved with his family to St. Paul, where he has lived since 2009.

He came into policing step by step. He began as a St. Paul Police Explorer, a youth program, and started as a community service officer in 2011. In 2014, after finishing college, he became the department's first officer of Karen ethnicity. St. Paul police say he was the first Karen officer in the state. He later worked patrol and in the forensic services unit, and at the time of his promotion he was in the traffic and pedestrian safety unit and returning to forensics. In 2024 he said St. Paul police had five other Karen officers. That year MPR also described him as a leader at the Karen Organization of Minnesota; he is not on the board list KOM shows as of October 2026.

Eh Tah Khu of KOM told MPR that Karen officers who are known in the community help people who feel nervous around police. The Pioneer Press reported that Khu called the promotion "an achievement for the community."
keyFacts: Spent his first 3 years in Myanmar and about 15 in Thai refugee camps; reported as 32 in February 2024.
2009: Moved to St. Paul at 18.
Police Explorer, community service officer from 2011, patrol officer, forensic services officer technician.
2014: First Karen officer in the St. Paul Police Department.
February 2024: Promoted to sergeant.

people.name: Myra Dahgaypaw
people.field: Human rights advocacy, U.S. foreign policy
body: Myra Dahgaypaw was, in the words of a 2015 interview, born as an internally displaced person. She was born in Karen State, Burma, and said, "my villages were burned down many times." Her family moved and rebuilt again and again, and at times she hid from Burmese troops in caves in the jungle. Her parents were killed when she was very young, and her father's younger brother raised her. Her oldest brother, his wife and his daughter were also killed, in the mid-1990s according to the interview.
In high school she joined the Karen Women's Organization, which set the course of her life. In April 2009 she appeared before the U.S. House Tom Lantos Human Rights Commission at a hearing on Burma.

She spent twelve years with the U.S. Campaign for Burma in Washington, D.C., as campaign coordinator, policy advisor and managing director, and she helped prepare petitions urging the Obama administration to act on crimes against humanity in Burma. As of October 2026, the Campaign's site lists her as its Board Advocacy Lead and as Senior Partnership Officer for International Justice and Accountability at the Unitarian Universalist Service Committee, whose own page says she oversees its Burma work.
Her work shapes U.S. policy on matters that reach Minnesota families, including refugee admissions, sanctions and aid to people still in Burma.
keyFacts: Born in Karen State, Burma, displaced from birth; raised by an uncle.
Joined the Karen Women's Organization in high school.
April 23, 2009: Appeared at a Tom Lantos Human Rights Commission hearing on Burma.
12 years with the U.S. Campaign for Burma.
Senior Partnership Officer, Unitarian Universalist Service Committee.
people.connectToWork: When someone has lived through violence or loss, how would your process leave room for what they have also led and accomplished?

people.name: Ehtalow Zar
body: In December 2024, Ehtalow Zar taught the students in her Karen advisory class at Johnson Senior High in St. Paul how to cook Karen porridge. A cooking lesson became a lesson in history and community.

Zar came to the U.S. not knowing English. She went through St. Paul Public Schools and was the first in her family to go to college. Along the way a professor told her that her English wasn't good enough to teach. She became a teacher anyway, starting as an associate educator in her home district. Teaching Sunday school kept her speaking and reading Karen.

As reported in January 2025, she taught math at Johnson along with a Karen advisory class and a Karen language class for Karen speakers. Students from other St. Paul high schools joined the language class virtually.

Before 2023, heritage language teachers relied on temporary permissions, which were limited. A 2023 state law created a program to help them get licensed, and its first cohort had 47 teachers. Zar used her ESL license and her curriculum and community work to build a portfolio, with four friends working alongside her. State officials said she was one of the first two people licensed to teach Karen in Minnesota, and possibly the country.
She has said of her students, "They feel like they're not proud of where they're from," and she wants to change that.
keyFacts: Arrived in the U.S. without knowing English.
First in her family to attend college.
2023: Minnesota created a heritage language licensing program; first cohort of 47 teachers.
January 2025: Reported as one of the first two teachers licensed to teach Karen in Minnesota.
people.connectToWork: Which of your rules assume that a skill only counts if it comes with a particular credential? Who does that shut out, and what would you check?

people.name: Remona Htoo
body: In January 2021, Remona Htoo stood by Como Lake in St. Paul with a small bilingual book she had made. My Little Legs tells an outdoor story for toddlers in English and Karen. Its main character, a little girl in a traditional Karen shirt, was inspired by her daughter Emma. She wrote it because she could not find children's books in Karen.

Sahan Journal reported in 2022 that only 32 Karen-language books were listed in U.S. libraries' WorldCat catalog, and that the St. Paul Public Library had published three Karen children's books since 2015.

Htoo spent ten years in a refugee camp in Thailand. In 2007, when she was 12, her family was resettled in Idaho. While at a small Christian university there she began visiting the Sawtooth Mountains, and she told Sahan Journal that hiking was "a healing mechanism for me." She later married a Karen man from St. Paul and moved to Minnesota, and the family lives on the city's east side.

She self-published the book with illustrations by local artist Mikayla Johnson, and she also sells stickers showing women of color in the outdoors. With her daughter she has explored Hidden Falls and Crosby Farm parks, the Superior Hiking Trail, and national parks such as Glacier. In 2024 she appeared in an episode of Minnesota PBS's Four Strangers, which says she has written two books and asks what home means to someone who cannot return to where she is from.
keyFacts: Spent 10 years in a Thai refugee camp.
2007: Resettled with her family in Idaho at age 12.
Moved to St. Paul after marrying; lives on the east side.
About 2021: Self-published My Little Legs, in English and Karen, for ages 1 to 3.
2024: Featured in Minnesota PBS's Four Strangers.
people.connectToWork: What in your office, your materials or your outreach would tell a family that their language is expected here, and how would you check?

people.name: Chris Tunbaw
body: Outside Mandalay Kitchen on University Avenue in St. Paul is a mural of an older woman, Daphne Tun Baw, the grandmother of chef Chris Tunbaw. She died just before the restaurant opened in November 2023, and he dedicated it to her. Inside, diners order mohinga, a noodle soup made from his mother's recipe, along with tea leaf salad, pumpkin curry and a weekend "Chapli Burger", his take on a Jucy Lucy.

Tunbaw is Karen. He grew up in what he called a "melting pot" near the Burma-Thailand border. CBS Minnesota reports that his family fled in 1996 and lived in a Thai refugee camp for a few years. Racket says he immigrated in the late 1990s, and CBS puts his arrival about 25 years before 2025, so reports range from the late 1990s to about 2000, which makes his family among the earliest arrivals from Myanmar.

He told CBS in 2024 that the restaurant is not a way to define what Burmese or Thai food is, and that "cultural representation is really important." Its menu follows the path of his life, adding dishes he came to love growing up in Minnesota.

He has also spoken publicly about immigration. When the federal government moved in November 2025 to end Temporary Protected Status for Myanmar, he told CBS, "I think everybody's still in shock," and said, "It's almost like sending them to their fate." Sahan Journal reported that a federal judge sided with the government on August 7, 2026, and that about 1,200 Minnesotans from Myanmar lost that status. As of October 2026 the restaurant's website says it is open.
keyFacts: 1996: Family fled Myanmar; lived in a Thai refugee camp for a few years.
Late 1990s to about 2000: Arrived in St. Paul (reports differ).
November 2023: Opened Mandalay Kitchen at 383 University Ave. W., St. Paul.
Dedicated the restaurant to his grandmother, Daphne Tun Baw, whose mural is on the building.
November 2025: Spoke publicly about the end of Temporary Protected Status for Myanmar.

people.name: Eh Taw Dwe
people.field: Public health, mental health advocacy, community leadership
body: In May 2008 a cyclone killed many people in Burma. In St. Paul, a public health translator named Eh Taw Dwe told MPR News that the true toll "will never, ever be counted." Of the Karen people still there, he said, "I feel like I am one of them."

Before he came to Minnesota, Eh Taw Dwe joined the armed struggle against Burma's military government. MPR reported that he was arrested, beaten and nearly executed. In 2002 he fled across the Thai border under gunfire with his wife, who was pregnant at the time. A later profile says he came to the United States in 2004 as a political refugee.

Soon after arriving in Minnesota he was hired by the St. Paul–Ramsey County Department of Public Health. He worked with Patty Shannon at the University of Minnesota to develop a mental health screening tool for Karen refugees. An undated profile calls him vice chair of the board of the Karen Organization of Minnesota; he is not on the board list KOM shows as of October 2026. He has spoken about Karen history to government, civic and business groups, and gave a presentation for torture treatment programs.
In 2010 he was one of the Minnesota organizers of Karen New Year. "The Karen people, they are pretty organized with counting the year and the history," he told MPR.
keyFacts: 2002: Fled Burma across the Thai border.
2004: Came to the U.S. as a political refugee.
Translator, St. Paul–Ramsey County Department of Public Health.
Helped develop a mental health screening tool for Karen refugees with the University of Minnesota.
Former vice chair, KOM board.
2010: An organizer of the Minnesota Karen New Year.

people.name: Mahn Robert BaZan
people.field: Faith, community leadership, former Karen resistance leader
body: For 30 years, Mahn Robert BaZan was a Karen guerrilla leader in Burma. Then he changed course. "I changed my strategy to nonviolent organization," he told Minnesota Lawyer in 2010.

He was born on November 27, 1941, the eldest of six children of Mahn Ba Zan, a former chairperson of the Karen National Union. By the account of the Karen Organization of Minnesota, he joined the Karen People's Liberation Army in 1964 and held several command roles. In 1997 he founded the Karen Solidarity Organization in Bangkok, to promote nonviolent efforts and help Karen students study abroad.

The United Nations granted him refugee status in 2000, and an uncle in St. Paul sponsored his move. He and his family arrived in August 2000. In Minnesota he helped establish the Karen Community of Minnesota in 2002 and 2003, the volunteer group from which KOM later grew, and he organized Karen New Year, Karen National Day and Martyr's Day events in Minnesota and other states. His family was among the first to join First Baptist Church in downtown St. Paul. He credited its pastor, Bill Englund, with making Karen families feel at home. "We love him, we respect him," he said.

In 2014, as an advisor to the Karen community in Minnesota, he publicly urged the Karen National Union to set a timeframe for ceasefire talks with Burma's government. He died of lung cancer at his home in St. Paul on May 11, 2018. A KOM program manager said, "He never thought about himself, always about the community."
keyFacts: November 27, 1941: Born.
Karen guerrilla leader for 30 years; 1997: founded the Karen Solidarity Organization in Bangkok.
2000: Granted refugee status by the UN; arrived in the U.S. in August.
2002–2003: Helped establish the Karen Community of Minnesota.
May 11, 2018: Died at home in St. Paul.

people.name: Hta Thi Yu Moo
people.field: Folk and traditional arts (weaving), arts program leadership
body: On Wednesdays, in the basement of the East Side Freedom Library in St. Paul, Karen weavers sit at backstrap looms and work cotton thread into bags, shirts and dresses. Hta Thi Yu Moo coordinates them. In 2026 Sahan Journal watched her help a community member set up his loom while teenagers worked beside master weavers.

She was born in a refugee camp in Thailand in 1994 and moved to Minnesota with her family in 2007. She began at the Karen Organization of Minnesota as a youth development coordinator and was promoted in 2017. In summer 2018 she organized a five-week youth weaving class, ending in a student showcase at the library, with funding from the Minnesota State Arts Board. In July 2025 she took four weavers to the Smithsonian Folklife Festival in Washington, D.C., the program's first event out of state. By 2026 the circle had met weekly for 12 years by Sahan Journal's count (the Smithsonian says women formed it in 2015, which would make it about 11), and that summer's youth camp ran five weeks with eight Karen teens.

She has described the circle's goals as empowering Karen weavers, showing their work, helping adults keep the practice alive in Minnesota, and connecting young people with their culture. As of October 2026, KOM lists her as its Weaving and Caregivers Program Coordinator, so she is also the contact for its support for family caregivers.
keyFacts: 1994: Born in a refugee camp in Thailand; 2007: moved to Minnesota.
2017: Promoted to coordinate KOM's weaving program.
2018: Organized a five-week youth weaving class and showcase.
July 2025: Took weavers to the Smithsonian Folklife Festival.
2026: Coordinates the weekly circle and KOM's Caregivers Program.
people.connectToWork: If you want to reach older adults, which gatherings already exist where they are teachers and not clients, and how would you learn about them without taking them over?

people.name: Paw Kaw Yee
body: In summer 2026, at a youth weaving camp in St. Paul, a 13-year-old student had finished two bags and started a third. Teaching beside her were the circle's master weavers, among them Paw Kaw Yee, who has woven since she was a teenager.

Paw Kaw Yee learned at Noh Poe, a refugee camp in Thailand. Today she is part of the Karen Weaving Circle run by the Karen Organization of Minnesota, which the Minnesota Legacy site describes as a collective of refugee women keeping their weaving alive and passing it to first-generation youth. Its master weavers supervise students as they set up backstrap looms, choose patterns and stitch finished pieces. One student said she learned "persistence and how to be patient with myself."

Paw Kaw Yee has explained her goal simply: to "keep our heritage alive, just like how our parents kept it alive." She said she hopes students will learn to work on their own and teach others "when we get too old."
keyFacts: Has woven since her teens, beginning at Noh Poe refugee camp in Thailand.
Master weaver with KOM's Karen Weaving Circle, St. Paul.
2026: Taught at the circle's five-week youth camp.

people.name: Ehkhudah Zar
body: On Saturday, April 25, 2026, the Paramount Theatre in Austin, Minnesota, presented a Karen legend on stage in English. The play was Muyehpen, by playwright and performer Ehkhudah Zar. Sahan Journal described it as one of the first English adaptations of a story kept secret because of fears of cultural persecution in Southeast Asia.

The legend follows Muyehpen, a girl born by magic and destined to bring peace to her people. Her fate turns dark when King Rama V of Siam, today's Thailand, is told that only her sacrifice can lift a curse that has lasted for generations. Exposed Brick Theatre presented the Austin production with pay-what-you-can tickets starting at $1.

Zar first staged the play with the same company in May 2023 at the Historic Mounds Theatre in St. Paul, and she played the title role. She told MPR the story had been passed down for generations in her family, and that she heard it again while visiting her grandmother in Thailand after college.
keyFacts: May 19–27, 2023: Premiere at the Historic Mounds Theatre, St. Paul; Zar played the title role.
April 25, 2026: Presented at the Paramount Theatre, Austin, Minnesota.
Described as one of the first English adaptations of the legend.
people.connectToWork: When a family offers you a story, not a timeline, how does your process make room for it, and what would you need to change in how you take notes?

institutions.name: Karen Organization of Minnesota
body: On December 30, 2008, a Karen community organization in the Twin Cities received its nonprofit status. The Karen Organization of Minnesota describes itself as the first social services agency in the country founded by Karen refugees from Burma.

KOM grew out of volunteer work. Karen leaders set up the volunteer Karen Community of Minnesota in 2003, and Vietnamese Social Services helped its members train and organize. In 2009 KOM received its first grants, hired its first executive director, Wilfred Tun Baw, and started with four staff serving 50 to 60 people a day, when about 3,000 Karen lived in Minnesota by its count. By 2011, when it opened its first youth program, it counted more than 5,000.

Today KOM says it serves over 3,000 clients a year and that most of its staff and board come from the communities it serves. Its programs include new-arrival services, adult career training, MNsure outreach, a caregivers program, mental health and family relationships, a Karen chemical dependency program, family planning, after-school and summer programs for youth, and walk-in services. It also carries culture through its Karen Weaving Circle and youth dance. In November 2025 its board named Alice Buckner executive director.
keyFacts: December 30, 2008: Nonprofit status.
2009: First grants and first executive director; four staff.
2011: First youth program.
Says it serves over 3,000 clients a year.
November 2025: Alice Buckner named executive director.

institutions.name: Karen Culture Organization of Minnesota
body: By its own account, the Karen Culture Organization of Minnesota was founded in 2008 to support the growing Karen population in the state. Its stated mission is to preserve and promote K'nyaw (Karen) culture and to create "a safe and welcoming space for our community."

The group teaches traditional dance and organizes cultural celebrations that bring generations together. Its programs are arranged by age: kids 5 to 12, youth 13 to 24, adult men 25 and older, and elder women 40 and older. As of October 2026 its site names Kyaw Kyaw Lwin as executive director and Po Eh as associate director.

Its partners include Saint Paul Public Schools, the Karen Organization of Minnesota, the Karen Community of Minnesota, the Karen Buddhist Association of Minnesota, The Urban Village, Karen cultural groups in the U.S., Thailand and Myanmar, and local Karen stores. That list crosses Christian and Buddhist groups and stays connected to the border region.
keyFacts: 2008: Founded in Minnesota, by its own account.
Mission: preserve and promote K'nyaw (Karen) culture.
Programs by age group, including adult men and elder women.
Leadership: Kyaw Kyaw Lwin, Po Eh.
institutions.connectToWork: If you treat one organization as your way to reach a whole community, who would you miss, and which other groups would you ask about?

institutions.name: Karen Football Association
body: In February 2020, boys' and girls' youth teams from the Karen Football Association were headed to the National Futsal Championships in Kansas City. FOX 9 reported they were the first all-Karen teams at the event, facing 178 other teams from 17 states. "It hasn't happened to the Karen community before," player Tina Million said. Another player, Ehku Say, said, "Not every Karen has the same opportunity like us."

According to FOX 9, Kyle Johnson had started the association just over a year earlier, because traditional clubs can cost too much for some refugee families and some lack reliable rides to practice. Its own site now describes a nonprofit based in Minnesota, with men's and women's teams, a development academy that takes players from age 4, and a digital marketing program.

In 2025 its women's team played its first season in the United Premier Soccer League, and Sahan Journal reported it was the league's first team focused on Karen women. The roster included teenagers, single mothers and players hoping to turn professional. The Karen Organization of Minnesota lists the association as the governing body for the Karen men's and women's national teams.
keyFacts: About 2019: Started by Kyle Johnson.
February 2020: Boys' and girls' teams at the National Futsal Championships.
2025: Women's team's first season in the United Premier Soccer League.
Runs a youth academy and men's and women's teams.

institutions.name: PACER Center
body: PACER Center is a Minnesota center for families of children with disabilities. According to a Family Voices brief, it has supported families and children with all disabilities since 1977 and is staffed mostly by parents of children with disabilities. The brief describes a language access plan updated each year, and a practice of adapting materials rather than only translating them, such as producing audio for people who do not read their first language. It also says PACER's multicultural staff serve as advocates and should never be asked to be the interpreters.

In January 2024 PACER announced seven parent documents in Karen, on topics including the special education process, IEP goals and how families can take part in a child's education. As of October 2026, its redesigned website shows sections in Spanish and Somali and the Karen documents could not be found there, so ask for them at 952-838-9000. PACER's contact page says it can arrange interpreters in multiple languages.
PACER is not a Karen-run organization. It is a general disability resource that has offered Karen-language materials.
keyFacts: Since 1977, staffed primarily by parents of children with disabilities.
January 2024: Seven parent documents released in Karen.
Interpreters available on request.
institutions.connectToWork: When you hand someone a translated document, how do you know it can be read and that it made sense? What would you offer instead?

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Karen means people of the ethnic group native to Burma (Myanmar) and Thailand, who differ widely by generation, religion, dialect, region of origin, years in refugee camps and literacy. This review did not find a Minnesota or U.S. study of how Karen families understand disability. What follows draws on a Minnesota Department of Health toolkit, a focus-group study that does not focus on disability, a study in rural Karen State in Myanmar known only from its project summary, and a 2005 report on the camps in Thailand.
questions: Which language do you want to use, and do you prefer to read it, hear it or see it?
How do you and your family understand what's going on? What words do you use for it?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Who gave it to you, do you agree with it, and has it helped or got in the way?
What would you want a label or an assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
If you would like to share it, what do you understand to have caused this, and what do you think would help?
Who helps you make decisions like this one? Would you like any of them here, and is there anyone you do not want involved?
Is faith or a pastor, monk or other leader important to you in this? Would you like them involved?
Who helps with care right now, and how do work hours and other demands affect that?
Did you go to school or get any disability services in Burma or in a camp in Thailand? What was that like?
Have past experiences with officials, soldiers or police affected how you feel about coming to us? What would make this feel safer?
For a Deaf person: which sign language do you use, and where did you learn it?

context.heading: Language, reading and translated words
body: The Minnesota Department of Health's Karen Culture and Foods toolkit (August 2025), written by Clara Tunwin, a Karen-American advocate, warns that it cannot describe every person. It estimates that more than 20,000 Karen refugees live in Minnesota, mostly in Ramsey County, with smaller communities in Freeborn, Lyon, Nobles, Kandiyohi and Mower counties. It says S'gaw Karen is the most widely understood and is the best one to request for translation, and that other dialects, such as West Pwo, East Pwo and Bwe, have their own writing systems. It estimates literacy at 30 to 40 percent, says such data are hard to collect, and says most children raised in Minnesota likely do not read Karen.

The toolkit also says modern health terms are newly constructed, so words vary by translator. No source was found that lists Karen words for disability, or says which words carry stigma, and terms such as waiver, IEP and PCA may raise the same problem. Ask the interpreter and the person which words they use, and do not assume that a written translation will be read. Offer spoken explanations, pictures or audio.

sources.label: Minnesota Department of Health, Karen Culture and Foods (Clara Tunwin, Aug. 20, 2025)

context.heading: Interpretation is the barrier the research documents
body: A study of four focus groups with 40 Karen refugees in an unnamed Midwestern city, split by gender and language, reported that "poor or improper interpretation has increased obstacles" to health care (Power and Pratt, 2012, abstract). It is one small sample, and it was not about disability.

A related article describes Karen patients at a St. Paul family medicine clinic (Power and colleagues, Minnesota Medicine, 2010). Only its abstract was available, and it does not address disability. In practice, use a trained interpreter rather than a child or relative, and ask the person to explain back key terms such as waiver, assessment and guardian.

sources.label: Power and Pratt, International Journal of Migration, Health and Social Care (2012), abstract
Power and colleagues, Minnesota Medicine (2010), abstract

context.heading: What a study in rural Karen State found
body: A Japanese-funded project led by Makoto Kono (2018 to 2023) visited 1,895 households in 10 villages in rural Karen State, Myanmar, and interviewed 10 people with disabilities and their families. Its summary names relatives as a safety net, mixed relationships with neighbors, and religion and refugee camps among the sources of support.

This study is known here only from its project summary. It concerns a related population in a very different setting, and it does not tell you about a family in Minnesota. It does not treat religion as a cause of stigma. No source found explains disability through spirits, karma or fate, so do not assume any family holds such a belief.

sources.label: Kono and colleagues, Needs for Persons with Disabilities to live in rural Karen, KAKEN project summary (18K11784)

context.heading: Schooling and services in the camps
body: A 2005 report by Aye Aye Mortimer in Enabling Education described camps then holding more than 90,000 Karen people. It says a Karen Sign Language was developed with video, that Karen braille programs existed in some camps but not all, and that disabled children who enrolled in school often dropped out because of poor teacher training. A local group, WEAVE, worked with parent groups on identifying impairments early but lacked funding to reach every camp.

This is more than 20 years old and does not describe the camps today. It suggests questions rather than answers: someone may never have been assessed, and a Deaf adult may use Karen Sign Language and not ASL. Not having used a service before is not the same as refusing one.

sources.label: Mortimer, Enabling Education 9, EENET (2005)

context.heading: Family, faith and who helps
body: The Department of Health toolkit says Karen Minnesotans practice Christianity, Buddhism and animism or traditional spiritual practices, and links the yearly Wrist Tying ceremony to traditional beliefs. It says people often confide in pastors and monks and ask for prayers and blessings, and that most would not be offended if a provider asks about faith. It describes foods, turmeric, lime, lemon and honey used for illness and discomfort. Nothing found suggests that faith and formal services conflict, so ask what the person already does and offer to include a faith leader if they want that.

The toolkit also describes a "village" of extended family and neighbors who help new mothers, and says this support has weakened in the United States because people are working to make a living and many fathers have no parental leave. It calls this a socio-economic cause. Do not assume that extended family can cover care. Ask, and hear directly from the disabled person even when a relative speaks first.

sources.label: Minnesota Department of Health, Karen Culture and Foods (Clara Tunwin, Aug. 20, 2025)

context.heading: Topics to raise with care
body: The toolkit says addiction, suicide and mental health "still carry a lot of stigmas" and that some people see them as a character flaw, and that remarks about when someone will die can be very upsetting. It also says some people avoid eye contact out of shyness, and that handshakes are fine. These are one author's general observations, and they will not fit everyone. When you need to raise mental health, prognosis or end-of-life care, explain why you are asking, use neutral words, and do not predict when someone will die.

In August 2026 Sahan Journal quoted the executive director of the Karen Organization of Minnesota, who said federal immigration interviews were bringing back memories of interrogations in the Thai camps for her clients. Check what a meeting may feel like before reading a missed appointment as lack of interest. Check shifts, rides and cost as well.

sources.label: Minnesota Department of Health, Karen Culture and Foods (Clara Tunwin, Aug. 20, 2025)
Sahan Journal, Refugees from Myanmar lose TPS protections (Aug. 18, 2026)

context.heading: Who is missing from this page
body: No Karen disabled leader, self-advocate or disability advocate documented in an accessible source was found, so none is profiled here. That says something about what has been written down, not about who exists. Do not treat any one person or organization as speaking for everyone.

communityRoutes.name: Karen Organization of Minnesota, Caregivers Program
communityRoutes.purpose: Supports unpaid in-home caregivers of adults over 60 or adults with neurological dysfunction with counseling, training, support groups, temporary substitute care and transportation. Funded through the Metropolitan Area Agency on Aging. The coordinator is Hta Thi Yu Moo, 651-202-3107.

communityRoutes.name: Karen Organization of Minnesota, Mental Health and Family Relationships and Karen Chemical Dependency Program
communityRoutes.purpose: Community health programs listed by KOM alongside family planning and MNsure outreach. Call to ask what is open and who can take part.

communityRoutes.name: PACER Center, Karen parent documents
communityRoutes.purpose: Seven parent documents in Karen on special education and family involvement, released in 2024. They are not easy to find on its current website, so call 952-838-9000. Interpreters can be arranged on request.

organizations.intro: The Minnesota Department of Health estimated in 2025 that more than 20,000 Karen refugees live in the state, and Sahan Journal reported about 22,000 people from Myanmar in 2026. Census data label Karen people as Burmese, so these are estimates. In 2019 an APM Research Lab researcher told MPR News that nearly 95 percent of Burmese Minnesotans lived in Ramsey County, and families have also moved to Albert Lea, Austin, Marshall and Willmar, where the Karen community in Albert Lea bought a church in 2018 that became Zion Karen Baptist. The list below is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts. No Minnesota-based Karen-language newspaper, radio show or cable program was found. Ask people what they follow.

entries.name: Karen Community of Minnesota
entries.purpose: A volunteer-led body set up in 2003, which KOM's history calls the community's governing body. It plans events such as Karen New Year and Martyrs' Day, and KOM grew out of it. Its main channel is Facebook.
entries.linkLabel: Listing and Facebook link on the Karen Organization of Minnesota site

entries.name: The Urban Village
entries.purpose: Works with Karen and Karenni young people through academic support, mentoring, a community space, an artist collective and a Karen Archive of narratives. Its team has also made trips to Kawthoolei, in eastern Myanmar, since the 2021 coup. The newest dated items on its site are from 2023, and KOM and the Karen Culture Organization still list it.

entries.name: Trinity Karen Baptist Church
entries.purpose: A Karen Baptist congregation with a weekly Sunday service. Marner Saw, profiled on this page, was a leader here.

entries.name: Karen Gospel Baptist Church
entries.purpose: A St. Paul congregation formed as a nonprofit in 2016. A grant record shows it receiving funding in December 2025. No website of its own was found.

entries.name: Sahan Journal
entries.purpose: The most regular coverage found of Karen Minnesotans, including immigration, weaving, sports, teachers and movement to Greater Minnesota. Multicultural, not specific to Karen people.

entries.name: MPR News
entries.type: Public radio and online, in English
entries.purpose: Statewide news that has covered Karen New Year, resettlement, the arts, Karen police officers and youth addiction.

entries.name: Karen Organization of America
entries.purpose: Formed in August 2018 from the merger of the Karen Organization of the United States of America and the Karen American Organization. Aims to keep Karen history and traditions alive and help refugees adjust. No website of its own was found.
entries.linkLabel: New York State Senate resolution recognizing it (2025)

entries.name: American Baptist Churches USA
entries.purpose: A Baptist denomination. Its Home Mission Societies translated six church leadership workshops into Karen in 2010, including one on preventing child abuse in churches.

entries.name: Karen Organization of San Diego
entries.purpose: Works on education and well-being for ethnic minority refugees from Burma in San Diego. Its site listed events in August and September 2026.

entries.name: EMBARC
entries.purpose: Founded in 2012 by refugees from Burma to serve refugees in Iowa. Runs language helplines, English classes, interpretation, crisis and advocacy services, and a refugee parent navigator program.

entries.name: Karen National Union
entries.purpose: A Karen political organization working toward a federal democratic Burma. It is not a service provider and does not speak for Karen Minnesotans, but it is part of the background to the news people follow.

entries.name: Karen Women's Organization
entries.purpose: Says it was established in 1949. Runs education, social welfare, health and organizing programs with women in refugee camps and displaced people inside Burma. Myra Dahgaypaw, on this page, joined it in high school.

entries.name: Karen Human Rights Group
entries.purpose: Trains villagers in southeast Burma to document abuses and publishes their accounts. It posted a report as recently as October 23, 2026.

entries.name: KIC News
entries.type: Online news, video and radio, in Burmese and Karen
entries.purpose: Founded in 1997. Its office in Hpa-an closed after the 2021 coup and moved back to the border. It was posting news on October 30, 2026. Its online radio service, Radio Karen, broadcasts in Karen, but radiokaren.org showed as unavailable on the same date.
entries.linkLabel: History of the Karen Information Center

entries.name: Karen News
entries.purpose: Started in 2011 by Karen journalists, with early funding from Union Aid Abroad-APHEDA. Covers issues affecting Karen communities in Burma and abroad.

entries.name: Democratic Voice of Burma
entries.type: Satellite TV and online, in Burmese and English
entries.purpose: Began in 1992 as shortwave radio from Norway. After the 2021 coup the junta revoked its license and it continued in exile and online. Covers Myanmar daily.

entries.name: RFA Burmese
entries.purpose: Radio Free Asia halted news production on October 31, 2025, after federal funding cuts. Its Burmese page was carrying stories dated October 29, 2026. Check its status before relying on it.
